Because decision-relevant model differences need not grow with elapsed time, we define Age of Intelligence (AoInt) as a model-version-relative, client-specific, and action utility distortion, and formulate synchronization as a tradeoff between stale-decision regret and refresh cost. Furthermore, we develop Kullback-Leibler-aware AoInt Synchronization (KL-AoIntSync), which accumulates output-distribution changes using client-specific unlabeled probes, whereas Parameter-aware AoInt Synchronization (Param-AoIntSync) uses a server-broadcast scalar parameter change. Then, we establish pathwise guarantees with fixed client distributions, action sets, and utilities. The numerical results show that calibrated Param-AoIntSync reduces joint synchronization cost by 6.15% relative to an Instant-Parameters policy while performing comparably to KL-AoIntSync.
item.dc:creator: Hui Wang, Seyyedali Hosseinalipour, Jacob Chakareski, Ming Shi

item.title: Agibot: An Open-Source Modular Swerve-Drive Robot Platform for Agricultural Robotics Research and Education
item.description: arXiv:2611.10235v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Agricultural production faces persistent labor shortages and increasing demand for automation, yet progress in agricultural robotics remains constrained by the limited availability of affordable, flexible, and accessible research platforms. This paper presents Agibot, an open-source, modular, low-cost agricultural robotics platform designed for autonomy research and experimentation, with potential applications in hands-on robotics education. The platform integrates four-wheel independent swerve drive, swappable computing, distributed embedded control, multimodal sensing, and configurable manipulation within a unified sense-plan-act-verify framework supporting perception, control, navigation, manipulation, and autonomous task verification. The platform was evaluated through representative row-crop navigation and manipulation tasks under varying lighting and soil conditions. Experiments demonstrated reliable lane following, autonomous row-to-row navigation, target identification, seed dispensing, plant manipulation, and closed-loop verification of task success. Its modular architecture supports independent testing, modification, and validation of autonomy components for rapid prototyping and experimentation. These proof-of-concept tasks, controller-tuning studies, and integrated trials demonstrate the platform's research capabilities, while its accessible and reconfigurable design supports its use for hands-on robotics education. By combining affordability, modularity, open-source accessibility, configurable manipulation, and end-to-end sense-plan-act-verify autonomy, Agibot provides a practical platform for agricultural robotics research, technology development, and workforce training.
item.dc:creator: Moeen Ul Islam, Bishal Adhikari, Kori Edwards, Lorien Harvey, J. Alex Thomasson, Dong Chen

item.title: Mobility Information Capacity of Multi-Robot Systems: Safety-Aware Maneuver Design
item.description: arXiv:2611.10298v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multiple robots operating in shared workspaces must adjust their speed, direction, and trajectories to coordinate with one another and respond to changing tasks and disturbances. The available maneuver freedom depends on the dynamics, uncertainty, and safety margins, even for a fixed fleet size and workspace. However, robot count, workspace occupancy, and task throughput do not quantify how much the fleet can vary its motion or how reliably these variations can be observed. We develop a mobility information capacity (MIC) framework that jointly characterizes these two aspects. Mobility information is defined as the mutual information between a joint maneuver sequence and its noisy trajectory observation, and MIC maximizes this quantity under maneuver-resource constraints. For a linear Gaussian maneuver-to-observation model with feedback dynamics, we characterize the finite-horizon information benchmark and derive its stationary long-horizon spectral limit, accounting for heterogeneous mobility gains, colored uncertainty, and temporally coupled maneuver costs. We further map workspace-boundary, inter-robot separation, and actuator chance constraints into coupled maneuver-covariance restrictions and derive conditions under which covariance optimization reduces to resource allocation across mobility modes. Finite joint maneuver codebooks are then constructed through individual risk screening and noise-whitened trajectory separation, with bounds linking sequence recovery error and achieved information to the capacity benchmarks. An aerial-robot simulation study evaluates spectral convergence, safety-aware allocation, finite-codebook identification, and fleet-size scaling. The resulting framework complements occupancy and task-throughput measures by quantifying the maximum observable maneuver freedom supported by a mobility system.
item.dc:creator: Weijie Yuan

item.title: Dynamic State Estimation from Sparse PMUs via Physics-Informed Graph Neural Operators
item.description: arXiv:2611.10468v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This paper proposes a physics-informed graph neural operator for power system dynamic state estimation. From a sparse, intermittent measurement window at a few generator buses, the operator estimates the rotor-angle and speed trajectories of all machines, unmeasured ones included, in one forward pass. A graph-attention encoder processes the measurements, and the swing equations are imposed as a hard constraint or as a soft one with a learned correction that absorbs model errors. It is trained on simulated measurements, without state labels. With several phasor measurement units, masked training hides one from the input but keeps it in the loss. On four transmission systems, simulations show that the operator is the most accurate estimator that neither optimizes per scenario nor uses state labels, except on the smallest system at large model errors, where tuned Kalman smoothers are better. Networks trained on simulated states are more accurate on the two smallest systems but not on the 118-bus system, where the operator is faster and more accurate than hard-constrained moving-horizon estimation. Under model errors, it matches or outperforms an optimization-based benchmark at a fraction of its cost. The results hold for a detailed machine model with exact parameters seen only through voltage phasors.
item.dc:creator: Huy Hoang Le, Haoguang Wang, Christian Moya, Marcos Netto, Guang Lin

item.title: Online Geometric Consistency Assessment of LiDAR Measurements via Recursive Bayesian Comparison
item.description: arXiv:2611.10566v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: LiDAR-based localization and mapping systems produce registered point clouds that serve as geometric measurements for downstream estimation and navigation. Registration errors introduce duplicated surfaces and structural deformation into these measurements. In the absence of an independent reference, online assessment relies on geometry accumulated from earlier measurements. Such assessment requires tolerance to sampling variation and an accumulation process in which observations enter the history only after evaluation. We therefore formulate a recursive Bayesian comparison that couples geometric assessment with history maintenance. A Normal-Inverse-Wishart model represents historical voxel geometry and its uncertainty, while a weak isotropic reference adapts to current sampling. Comparing the marginal predictive support of the same current points under both models yields Normalized Drift Evidence (NDE). Assessment precedes assimilation: positive NDE triggers an alarm and preserves the preceding historical state; otherwise, the current observations update the history. Across 14 real-world sequences totaling approximately 73 min from four platform types, alarms identified all nine corrupted sequences and were absent from all five consistent sequences. In four representative scenarios with event references, first alarms occurred within 0.9 s of the reference times, with no preceding alarms. Cross-backend evaluation demonstrates consistent responses to reconstructed geometry. Ablation and controlled perturbation results establish the roles of uncertainty modeling, recursive history, displacement, and geometric support. Mean processing time is 4.2--6.1 ms per update at 1 Hz. In ten UAV trials, alarms initiated odometry isolation, landing, relocalization, and mission continuation.
item.dc:creator: Mingqiao Han, Qigeng Duan, Xuchen Liu, Jinqiang Cui, Xi Chen, Ben M. Chen

item.title: From Discrete Snapshots to Geometric Entity: Motion-Native Channel Tracking for THz Near-Field XL-MIMO
item.description: arXiv:2611.10587v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Channel tracking in mobile terahertz (THz) near-field extremely large-scale multiple-input multiple-output (XL-MIMO) systems is challenging because spherical-wave propagation couples angle and range, leading to rapid and nonlinear channel evolution under sparse pilot observations. Existing approaches typically estimate pilot-local channel or position snapshots before applying temporal tracking or smoothing, making them vulnerable to information loss during snapshot formation. To break this bottleneck, we propose a paradigm shift from tracking discrete snapshots to estimating a holistic geometric entity, namely, one shared continuous UE trajectory over the tracking window. Specifically, we parameterize the trajectory using a low-dimensional cubic B-spline representation and directly couple the per-pilot profile likelihoods through this shared trajectory before any pilot-local position estimate is finalized, thereby inducing continuous near-field channel evolution. We further characterize the efficient geometric information supplied by each pilot observation and its aggregation in the shared spline-coefficient space. Based on this formulation, we develop a regularized maximum a posteriori estimator and a quadratic-penalty lifted solver that separates parallel pilot-local geometric updates from a structured global spline update. The resulting global system is banded and, for a fixed spline degree, admits linear-complexity factorization, enabling an efficient structured implementation. Simulations demonstrate consistently improved tracking accuracy over representative temporally refined baselines in the tested medium-to-high-SNR regime, together with a favorable accuracy--runtime trade-off. These results highlight the benefit of coupling sparse pilot observations through a shared continuous trajectory rather than temporally processing independently estimated snapshots.
item.dc:creator: Yuheng Fan, Chuang Yang, Mugen Peng

item.title: Worst-Case Contagion in Financial Networks: MILP Clearing and Robust Loss Analysis
item.description: arXiv:2611.10607v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study worst-case contagion losses in financial networks with interbank liabilities and common exposures to marketable assets. Existing linear-programming approaches provide exact stress-test values only within an insolvency-resilience margin, where all institutions remain solvent with respect to the external sector. We show that this margin is computed exactly by a finite family of linear programs, one per vertex of the uncertainty ball, whereas a single linear program based on the componentwise worst deterioration of external resources yields only a certified lower bound. We extend this framework beyond that margin in three directions. First, we derive an exact mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) formulation for the maximal clearing vector under arbitrary signed external net positions, providing a clearing oracle for robust stress testing when insolvency can occur. Second, we develop certified bounds on the worst-case loss beyond the margin, including insolvency-pattern enumeration, scenario lower bounds, fixed-pattern dual upper bounds, localized certificates, and a regime-generation procedure with monotone gap certificates. Third, we analyze the worst-case loss curve as a function of the perturbation radius. For $\ell_1$ and $\ell_\infty$ price-perturbation sets, the curve is convex, nondecreasing and piecewise linear up to the margin, with breakpoints generated by switches in worst-case shock directions, LP bases, and bank-level activity patterns. Beyond the margin, it remains nondecreasing and piecewise affine, but convexity may fail, the curve may jump upward, and the worst case need not be attained. The framework provides a certifiable MILP/LP methodology for parametric stress testing and interpretable diagnostics identifying the banks responsible for changes in systemic loss.
item.dc:creator: G. C. Calafiore, M. Della Rossa, A. Proskurnikov

item.title: Passivity-Guaranteed Variable Impedance and Compliance Control via Online Parameter Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2611.10778v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Variable impedance control enhances the interaction capability of robot manipulators by adapting impedance parameters online. However, time-varying impedance parameters may inject energy into the system and violate passivity, particularly when tasks demand rapid stiffness changes. Existing methods address this by increasing damping or limiting the stiffness profile, which often degrades the dynamic response. In this work, we propose a quadratic programming-based parameter optimization framework that guarantees passivity by modulating the desired inertia to compensate for energy injected by stiffness variations, while preserving a critically damped system. For the case of diagonal impedance matrices, we optimize the rates of change of inertia and stiffness subject to a passivity constraint formulated as a convex quadratic program. We extend the framework to compliance control, where the desired inertia is coupled to the robot's configuration-dependent inertia matrix. We use an eigendecomposition based on Cholesky factorization to optimize the spectral weights while maintaining passivity. Experiments on the Kinova Gen3 7-degree-of-freedom manipulator validate both methods with human interaction perturbations. Comparisons with an energy tank approach and a nonpassivity-based method demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves less conservative stiffness tracking without requiring an energy reservoir or damping overhead.
item.dc:creator: Huseyin Tugcan Dinc, Ersin Da\c{s}, Nikolas Thelenberg, Christian Ott

item.title: Modified CNN-Learned Surrogate Covariance With Krylov/Lanczos Subspace for DoA Estimation
item.description: arXiv:2611.10833v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recently, learning-based approaches have been employed to improve the robustness of subspace methods in DoA estimation. A Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) was used as a data-driven framework employing an autoencoder to generate a well-conditioned surrogate covariance optimized end-to-end through a differentiable classical estimator, such as the Root-MUSIC. The complete system is designed to estimate the directions of arrival based on a spectral decomposition using the EVD of this covariance matrix. In this work, a new approach is proposed by formulating the spectral stage of the Root-MUSIC algorithm in terms of the orthogonal complement of the signal subspace, thereby eliminating the need for the noise subspace and noise eigenvalues. Furthermore, the full EVD is replaced by a Lanczos tridiagonalization with reorthogonalization, reducing the overall computational cost.
item.dc:creator: R. Brandt, F. Rangel de Sousa, V. J. Brusamarello

item.title: Sampling-based Model Predictive Control as Sequential Monte Carlo Inference
item.description: arXiv:2611.10877v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Sampling-based model predictive control (MPC) is treated as a family of distinct algorithms: predictive sampling, MPPI, the cross-entropy method, and their biased, colored-noise, and annealed variants all sample control sequences and reweight them by cost. We show a single Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) inference algorithm implements them all, specified by three independent axes: the proposal, the update rule that reduces cost-weighted particles to a nominal plan, and the effective-sample-size threshold for resampling. We evaluate SMC-based planning on MuJoCo non-linear control, open-loop navigation through obstacle fields, 7-DoF motion planning, and non-prehensile push-T, in simulation and on a Franka FR3. Resampling combats particle degeneracy at long horizons. At a 28-knot horizon in our navigation domain it cut the collision rate by 30% over non-resampling baselines. Programmable proposals improve push-T success over perturbative baselines, improving from 1% to 100% in simulation and 10% to 90% on hardware.
item.dc:creator: Austin Garrett, Muyang Yan, Zachary Kingston

item.title: BRACE: Belief-guided Residual Adaptive Control for Safe Navigation under Unknown Disturbances
item.description: arXiv:2611.10938v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Disturbances encountered during autonomous navigation generally vary across space, often discontinuously, as obstacles redirect wind and changing terrain alters traction. Tracking controllers typically assume sufficient control authority to mitigate disturbances and maintain safety; the regime where this assumption fails remains underexplored. We present Belief-guided Residual Adaptive Control (BRACE), a hierarchical reinforcement learning (RL) framework for reach-avoid navigation under unknown, bounded, spatially varying disturbances. BRACE infers a disturbance belief from model prediction errors and uses that to condition a high-level policy that adapts the reference trajectory. The policy combines a nominal and a belief-guided residual term, trained jointly with a likelihood-ratio advantage reweighting heuristic. We evaluate BRACE in three simulated quadcopter environments with abruptly switching wind fields, and validate it on Crazyflie hardware with fan-generated disturbances. Across these settings, BRACE improves reach-avoid performance over model predictive control and RL baselines.
item.dc:creator: Jaeyoun Choi, Niklas Schmid, Oswin So, Augustinos Saravanos, Chuchu Fan

item.title: Floquet-Parameterized Koopman-MPC for Tracking Periodic Orbits
item.description: arXiv:2611.11050v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Designing real-time control for nonlinear systems to track periodic orbits can be challenging, especially for complex and coupled dynamical systems (e.g., tethered kites), where the true model parameters are hard to obtain. To address this, we propose a physics-informed Koopman learning approach that incorporates periodic-orbit stability directly into the learned linear predictor. The approach combines the underlying periodic structure of the dynamics along with periodic state-input trajectory data to learn physically consistent linear predictors (in lifted/observable space). We leverage Floquet theory, which studies the stability of periodic orbits in nonlinear systems, to obtain the periodic stability information of a given orbit via a monodromy matrix (i.e., the state transition matrix over an entire period). Subsequently, we impose open-loop monodromy constraints to learn Floquet-parameterized linear predictors using a least-squares Extended Dynamic Mode Decomposition (EDMD) formulation, thereby constraining the search space and aiding in Koopman learning. We then utilize these linear predictors to design a model predictive control (MPC) law for tracking periodic references. Finally, we evaluate the designed framework on a cartpole system under periodic forcing and compare it against a purely data-driven baseline.
item.dc:creator: Kartik A. Pant, Vishnu Vijay, Yufei Zhu, Xintong Deng, Taewoo Nam, Inseok Hwang

item.title: Analysis increments for model bias diagnosis and correction: Theoretical foundations
item.description: arXiv:2611.11162v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A common method for diagnosing and correcting model bias in weather and climate prediction is based on analysis increments: the difference between the analysis and the forecast at each data assimilation cycle. Their time average is used to estimate and correct the bias, and machine learning is increasingly used to map the forecast state to the increments, giving a state-dependent correction. Despite its widespread use, the method lacks theoretical foundations. We first analyse a Kalman filter whose forecast model has a constant bias. We show what the averaged increment measures, and prove that iterating the correction removes all of the bias seen through the observations; for linear dynamics, no method can identify the rest. We then extend the analysis to state-dependent biases. For linear dynamics, each increment records the model error over the filter's memory, as seen through the observations. We use this to determine what the increments measure when averaged over a long period, averaged over periods with similar slowly varying conditions, and used without averaging, as in machine-learned corrections. Numerical experiments confirm the theory for a linear model and suggest that its main conclusions carry over to the nonlinear Lorenz '96 model, including for a correction learned by a neural network.
item.dc:creator: Eviatar Bach

item.title: A Multistage Extension of Witsenhausen's Counterexample with Linear Signaling
item.description: arXiv:2611.11181v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study a multistage scalar extension of Witsenhausen's counterexample in which controller 1 observes the initial state exactly, whereas every subsequent controller observes only a local noise-corrupted state and does not inherit its predecessors' observations, so that every nonterminal action both regulates the state and shapes the signal available to the next controller. Restricting the signaling controllers to linear policies while leaving the terminal controller unrestricted, we compute the exact value within this class and reduce the optimization to a deterministic dynamic program in a single propagated variance. The optimal intermediate gains are shown to have a shrinkage form, and the value functions of that program are concave. For two stages, the benchmark admits a closed form on a matching locus, where for small effort weights it has two distinct minimizers, and at the standard parameter instance on that locus a two-point nonlinear policy strictly improves upon it. For three stages, numerical continuation at a reference instance reveals three distinct local minima, and two values of the initial variance at which the lowest of the three changes abruptly. Under the terminal-cost normalization we further prove, for every finite horizon, that the optimal linear value becomes asymptotically equal to the signaling-idle benchmark as the initial variance tends to infinity.
item.dc:creator: Quanyan Zhu, Tamer Ba\c{s}ar

item.title: K-PWM: Control-Oriented Structured Bilinear World Models under Partial Observation
item.description: arXiv:2611.11521v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: World models learn internal simulators of environment dynamics for prediction, planning, and control, yet learning them from limited, noisy, and partial observations remains challenging. While much progress has focused on pixel-based observations, many physical systems instead provide vector-valued measurements that reveal only part of the underlying state. We introduce K-PWM, a probabilistic world model for prediction and control under partial observation. K-PWM couples Koopman-bilinear latent dynamics with a nonlinear observation decoder and performs probabilistic latent-state inference through the learned model via extended Kalman filtering and smoothing, without a separately trained inference network. Its bilinear structure enables exact propagation of the maintained Gaussian belief through the latent transition and efficient rollouts for uncertainty-aware model predictive path integral (MPPI) control. For training K-PWM, we present a generalized expectation conditional maximization (GECM) procedure with closed-form updates for the generators, noise covariances, and latent prior, complemented by gradient-based decoder learning. A Koopman-consistent initialization selects the latent dimension from data and initializes the action-dependent dynamics. With limited training data, K-PWM achieves lower long-horizon prediction error than the evaluated baselines on partially observed Gymnasium MuJoCo systems, while substantially reducing training time relative to the strongest prediction baseline. On high-dimensional MuJoCo Menagerie robots, it achieves competitive tracking accuracy with low per-step computation times, demonstrating potential for real-time deployment. These results support structured probabilistic dynamics as a data- and compute-efficient approach to world modeling and control under partial observation.
item.dc:creator: Santosh Mohan Rajkumar, Sriram Narayanan, Samuel E. Otto, Debdipta Goswami

item.title: PA-SaR: Perception-Aware Learning, Control, and Coordination for Multi-Robot Search and Rescue
item.description: arXiv:2611.11648v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Autonomous SaR requires robots to explore unknown or partially known environments, avoid hazards, coordinate team activities, and guide discovered victims to safety. Improving individual capabilities of robots does not necessarily improve mission outcomes: safer motion can restrict the exploration behavior, faster discovery can increase the rescue demand, and effective guidance depends on victim responses. We introduce PA-SaR, a mathematical and architectural framework for coordinating heterogeneous local control, learning-based exploration, supervisory task allocation, and adaptive approach-lead victim guidance around mission-level objectives. PA- SaR distinguishes environmental ground-truth, robot-specific perceptions, and simulated victim behavior. This provides a common basis for integrating complementary mechanisms and analyzing their interactions across mission stages. We demonstrate the framework through single- and multi-robot simulation studies incorporating model-predictive and learning-based exploration, perception-based safety shielding, event-driven task allocation, and adaptive victim guidance. The results show trade-offs between collision avoidance and search completion, indicate that supervisory allocation improves search completion beyond information sharing alone, and demonstrate that increased exploration does not necessarily yield more rescues. Adaptive guidance increases rescues relative to continuous leading, without a detected improvement in mean or final victim trust or a reduction in mortality. These findings support evaluating local control, team coordination, and evacuation as related but distinct aspects of autonomous SaR within the considered simulation environments.
item.dc:creator: Jocubas Dimsa, Maria Grouev, Filip Keerberg, Nicolas Laplagne, Tigo Schutgens, Sven Schoonebeek, Anahita Jamshidnejad

item.title: ShadowBench-MCP: Measuring Shadow Invocations in MCP-Style Tool Routing
item.description: arXiv:2611.11720v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: LLM agents increasingly act as routers for tools, APIs, and software-supply-chain workflows, making an execution path - rather than generated text alone - a security-relevant model output. We study shadow invocation: a task-preserving request variant that causes an LLM router to select a riskier execution path, potentially skipping validation, provenance, staging, redaction, or audit controls even though the request does not ask for a malicious action. We introduce ShadowBench-MCP, a benchmark and metric suite that separates task preservation (TPSS), operational pressure (OPSS), and route-geometric drift (RGAS), and combines them in the pre-execution SODS score. In a focused policy-ablation study using a Groq-hosted qwen/qwen3-32b router, 120 routing decisions yield 96 original-versus-variant comparisons across six security-sensitive workflows. Efficiency-first routing produces a 29.2% shadow-invocation rate and 26.7% safety-tool skip rate. Policy-aware routing reduces these to 4.2% and 1.7%, respectively, corresponding to an 85.7% relative reduction in shadow invocations. Pre-execution signals distinguish shadow routes with ROC AUC up to 0.94. These results are early, single-router evidence of a policy-dependent routing-layer security effect, not a claim of universal vulnerability.
item.dc:creator: Eyhab Al-Masri, Wenjun Yang

item.title: A Bifurcation-Theoretic Framework for the Controllability of Emergent Intelligent Systems
item.description: arXiv:2611.11734v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Real-world intelligent systems must reconcile two demands: the adaptability conferred by emergence and the steerability required for accountable deployment. We show that these demands are governed by two distinct bifurcations on the same object and that, consequently, increased capability does not imply increased controllability. Emergence is a bifurcation of the capability variable $S$, with criterion $\Gamma:=\mathcal F'(0)>1$ equivalent to the existence of a unique positive stable fixed point of a self-consistency equation, following solely from the concavity of $\mathcal F$. Controllability is a bifurcation of the permission variable $c$, whose dynamics include an erosion term and exhibit a saddle-node fold with hysteresis as the gate criterion $\rho^\ast$ crosses unity. Three quantitative results follow: the critical exponent distinguishes families rather than classifying the transition; the gating-cost bound $K(M)\propto\log(1+M)$ grows with scope, not capability; and the fold threshold is $\gamma_c\approx4\mu\kappa$. Calibrated in both directions, the criteria reproduce the two-dimensional Ising transition, admit two true-feedback order parameters, and reject nine candidate quantities, supporting the conclusion that the order parameter is geometric rather than capability-related. Since permission cannot be endogenized and no deployed system has been measured to satisfy $\Gamma>1$ and $\rho^\ast>1$ simultaneously, increased capability does not imply controllability.
item.dc:creator: Hao Li, Shaowen Lu

item.title: Silinx: An Open, Browser-Based HDL Design Platform for Teaching Digital Systems on FPGA Boards
item.description: arXiv:2611.11741v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Many digital systems courses teach on FPGA boards whose vendor tool is no longer maintained: the Digilent Basys2 and Nexys2 (Xilinx Spartan-3E) and Nexys3 and Atlys (Spartan-6) need Xilinx ISE 14.7, discontinued since 2013 and hard to install on the computers and tablets students use today. The author presents Silinx, a free (AGPL-3.0) HDL design platform for teaching that keeps ISE's Project Navigator workflow but runs in a web browser with nothing to install. A module can be written in VHDL or Verilog, in C or C++ through Silinx HLS, which is compatible with AMD's Vitis HLS and passes all 73 of its introductory examples, or drawn as a schematic, an ASM chart, a state diagram, a Boolean function with its Karnaugh map, or a Petri net, from which its HDL is generated. Designs are checked with explanations written for beginners, simulated, run on an emulated board, built, and programmed onto a real board over WebUSB. The implementation flow is open and runs in the browser: Yosys and nextpnr compiled to WebAssembly, with Silinx's own device data, timing model and bitstream writer for the Spartan-3E and Spartan-6, built by black-box observation of ISE's documented tools; Lattice iCE40 boards use the existing open iCE40 tools, and further families are planned. ISE is the oracle: Silinx's bitstreams are byte-identical to those ISE writes for the same placed and routed design, and pass ISE's design rule check. Against ISE at the same optimization goal, the open flow uses 15% fewer slices with 14% shorter critical paths when optimizing for area, and 21% fewer slices with 8% shorter critical paths when optimizing for speed (geometric means over 45 open-source designs built by both flows). The author also describes how the platform was developed with AI coding agents under test-first project rules.
item.dc:creator: Pedro Malo

item.title: Graph-Sparse Distributed Predictive Control for Multi-Robot Motion Planning vianEdge-Consensus ADMM
item.description: arXiv:2611.11755v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This paper presents a distributed model predictive control (MPC) architecture for collision-avoiding motion planning of planar robots with double-integrator dynamics. To reduce coordination demands, a time-varying predicted conflict graph selects relevant pairwise interactions. The associated collision-avoidance constraints are convexified once per MPC update using warm-start trajectories, yielding a fixed convex quadratic program (QP). The resulting QP is then decomposed using an edge-consensus formulation of the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM), enabling parallel robot-local optimization and independent closed-form projections onto separating half-spaces. Execution is selectively supervised by a centralized high-order control barrier function (HOCBF) QP when the distributed candidate does not satisfy the direct-execution conditions. Evaluated in C++ simulations involving 8, 16, and 32 robots, the proposed architecture achieves collision-free execution and substantially improves computational scalability while maintaining task-level performance comparable to a centralized complete-graph baseline.
item.dc:creator: Josep Borras-Borras, Pablo Segovia, Carlos Ocampo-Martinez

item.title: Online Digital Twins: Data Assimilation and Control
item.description: arXiv:2611.12001v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The online assimilation of data and the application of controls are essential ingredients of the digital twin paradigm. In this paper, we formalize the online interaction between the physical process and its virtual digital representation in the setting of continuously arriving data from the physical process and a receding horizon virtual planning process, which provides the control for the physical process. Our mathematical formulation relies on a mean field representation of the data assimilation process as well as a mean field Pontryagin minimum principle for the optimal control problem. Such mean field formulations are computationally attractive because they allow for simultaneous implementation in terms of Hamiltonian interacting particle systems. A more detailed discussion is included for the ensemble Kalman-Bucy filter in combination with affine approximations of the receding horizon control laws. This paper sets out the mathematical framework, while a computational study is left for future research.
item.dc:creator: Sebastian Reich

item.title: Compact and Wide-Force-Range Magnetorheological Hand Exoskeleton for Kinesthetic Feedback in Teleoperation
item.description: arXiv:2611.12130v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Hand kinesthetic feedback is crucial for restoring and enhancing human perception of force and displacement in robotic hand teleoperation. Wide perception range of force feedback is vital in rendering objects of different stiffness, especially for high-stiffness rendering. However, existing approaches struggle to achieve wide range of force feedback while maintaining compact and wearable design. This paper presents a hand exoskeleton system employing magnetorheological (MR) brakes to provide a wide range kinesthetic feedback during teleoperation. The MR brake provides a braking torque ranging from 0.01 to 0.918 Nm, while maintaining a compact structure with a total mass of only 39.8 g. The proposed exoskeleton can render fingertip forces up to 21 N while maintaining back-driving force of 1.01 N. Experimental results show that the system allows users to discriminate object stiffness using kinesthetic feedback alone. In a tele-grasping task, when both conditions achieved a 100% success rate, kinesthetic feedback led to a 28.2% reduction in object contact force compared to visual feedback only, enhancing object safety and operator immersion. Questionnaire results further indicate that kinesthetic feedback improves reliability, realism, and user confidence during teleoperation.
item.dc:creator: Xianlong Mai, Rui Yu, Rui Chen, Daniele Leonardis, Wenbo Li, Domenico Chiaradia, Antonio Frisoli, Shuaishuai Sun

item.title: On necessary conditions for feedback stabilizability when the control space is a fiber bundle
item.description: arXiv:2611.12143v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Within control theory, a question of great interest is to understand when a stabilizing feedback exists. Building upon Krasnosel'ski\u{\i} and co-workers, necessary conditions for the existence of a continuous stabilizing feedback have been pioneered by Brockett and Coron, providing so-called adversarial and homological conditions, respectively. Kvalheim recently generalized their conditions from equilibria to compact attractors and---in line with earlier work by Coron---showed that when a control system can be identified with a vector bundle, the homology condition is stronger, that is, the homology condition implies the adversary condition. Kvalheim also showed that this comparison breaks when extending the case of vector bundles to fiber bundles. In this work, we propose and characterize an appropriate adversarial condition for control systems represented by fiber bundles. The homology condition, on the other hand, is already well-defined, showcasing its general applicability. With the generalized conditions at hand, we show that by appropriately relaxing the regularity of the feedback under consideration, that is, by allowing for mild discontinuities, the homology condition implies the adversarial condition for fiber bundles. Thereby, in this work, we extend these earlier comparative results.
item.dc:creator: Wouter Jongeneel, Martina Scolamiero, Karl Henrik Johansson

item.title: A Game-Theoretic MPC Planner for Cooperative and Adversarial Drone Coordination
item.description: arXiv:2611.12226v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present and evaluate a game-theoretic model predictive control planner for cooperative goal reaching and adversarial pursuit-evasion with drones. The planner combines 3D prediction, individual objectives, optional shared separation constraints and trajectory-tracking interfaces. A comparison of cooperative game solvers assesses their ability to find feasible trajectories that resolve conflicts. A computational study quantifies how number of drones, prediction horizon and move blocking affect computation time and numerical acceptance. Move blocking holds control inputs constant over groups of prediction steps, reducing the number of independent control variables and lowering computation time. Timing measurements identify the practical limits of real-time planning in the tested configurations. PyBullet simulations demonstrate cooperative goal reaching and pursuit-evasion. A laboratory flight complements the simulations by validating the trajectory-tracking interfaces on physical drones. The planner can serve as a basis for further evaluation and controller development.
item.dc:creator: Zden\v{e}k Bou\v{c}ek, Miroslav Fl\'idr

item.title: Safety-Constrained Intelligent Control of a 2-DOF Robotic Manipulator Using Control Barrier Functions
item.description: arXiv:2611.12378v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Control barrier function (CBF) filters depend on dynamic models that can be inaccurate when their parameters and external forces are uncertain. This paper investigates a radial basis function (RBF) neural network compensator whose output is shared by a Cartesian tracking controller and a joint-space CBF filter. An auxiliary state driven by the difference between requested and applied torques corrects the learning signal, reducing the direct influence of filter intervention on adaptation. A two-link manipulator is evaluated through constrained regulation, ablations, matched uncertainty and disturbance trials, and operating-range and timing studies. The results demonstrate that the proposed controller improves tracking while maintaining joint, velocity, and torque limits under parameter uncertainty, and that both the shared compensation and the auxiliary correction contribute to this improvement.
item.dc:creator: Gabriel da Silva Lima, Made Widhi Surya Atman, Wallace Moreira Bessa

item.title: Converse Lyapunov theorem for input-to-state stability of infinite-dimensional systems
item.description: arXiv:2611.12601v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We prove converse Lyapunov theorems for input-to-state stability (ISS) of a broad class of infinite-dimensional systems applicable to evolution equations in Banach spaces, boundary control systems, and delay systems. To this end, we employ a novel method that does not require constructing auxiliary closed-loop systems. We start by showing that ISS of a control system implies uniform global asymptotic stability of the same system with respect to trajectory-dominated inputs. Then, under an additional regularity requirement, we prove that an ISS Lyapunov function can be constructed. Based on our general result, we prove that for linear systems with unbounded $\infty$-admissible operators, ISS is equivalent to the existence of a Lipschitz continuous coercive ISS Lyapunov function.
item.dc:creator: Patrick Bachmann, Andrii Mironchenko

item.title: KL-Regularized Policy Iteration for Adaptive LQR: Gain Updates and Probing from One Policy Improvement
item.description: arXiv:2611.12741v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Policy-gradient methods for adaptive linear quadratic control improve the feedback gain of an unknown plant online by gradient-type steps computed from closed-loop data. A recent framework of such methods, policy-gradient adaptive control (PGAC), takes one gradient-type step per sample, which its indirect form computes from an estimated model and its direct form directly from the data. Because data generated by a fixed linear feedback cannot identify the plant, PGAC adds a probing perturbation to the input and leaves its covariance as a design parameter. We study the adaptive LQR problem through a KL-regularized formulation, in which the probing is the randomness of a Gaussian policy kept close to a Gaussian reference policy, so that the cost of the probing is part of the objective. One policy improvement of this formulation gives a gain update together with a probing covariance. We show that, for suitable references centred at the current gain, this gain update is exactly PGAC's Gauss-Newton or natural-gradient update with any step size below a bound. We repeat this policy improvement, each time against a tempered copy of the current policy, and refer to this scheme as KL-regularized policy iteration (KLPI). On a known plant and with tempering, the cost of KLPI's gains converges linearly to the optimal cost, and the probing covariance keeps a floor proportional to the regularization weight. On an estimated plant, under conditions like PGAC's (small updates and sufficiently informative data), the closed loop stays stable, the cost of the gains converges linearly up to a bias, and the probing covariance again keeps this floor. In simulations at equal probing cost, the shape of KLPI's probing covariance, which PGAC can adopt, lowers the extra cost caused by suboptimal gains on nearly all tested plants, whereas KLPI's use of past iterations in its gain update changes this cost little.
item.dc:creator: Ajinkya Bhole, Mohammad Mahmoudi Filabadi, Guillaume Crevecoeur, Tom Lefebvre

item.title: Sliding into Balance: Benefits of a Sliding Payload for Load Distribution and Disturbance Rejection in Dual-UAV Transportation
item.description: arXiv:2611.12754v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This paper analyzes the cooperative transportation of a payload suspended from two drones in which, instead of being attached to two independent ropes, the payload is allowed to slide along a single rope connecting both UAVs. First, a planar nondimensional dynamical model of the sliding motion with viscous friction is presented. Then, considering stationary drones, this configuration is compared with a fixed payload with the same total rope length, both at equilibrium and under disturbances. The analytical results show that the sliding payload equalizes the tension in both rope segments for any relative position of the drones, so that no rope loses tension at equilibrium; it doubles the region reachable by the payload and, except for low friction combined with a large drone separation, it enlarges the set of admissible disturbances. Finally, a dynamic simulation also shows that under realistic gusty wind profiles, the average tension imbalance between the drones is reduced with respect to the fixed-payload solution.
item.dc:creator: Jorge Vicente-Martinez (Universidad de Zaragoza), Francisco Jos\'e Ma\~nas-\'Alvarez (Universidad Nacional de Educaci\'on a Distancia), Edgar Ramirez-Laboreo (Universidad de Zaragoza)

item.title: Succinct Infinite-Horizon Lyapunov and LQR Value Problems Are BQP-Complete
item.description: arXiv:2611.12757v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Fundamental tasks in linear systems analysis and control require evaluating infinite-horizon output energies for autonomous systems and optimal value functions for controlled systems. These quantities are characterized by Lyapunov and algebraic Riccati equations, respectively. In this work, we study promise problems for their evaluation when the system matrices are sparse and represented succinctly by Boolean circuits specifying their nonzero entries, with input length polynomial in the logarithm of the system dimension. For dissipative autonomous systems with coordinate-vector initial states, we define the succinct Lyapunov value problem (SLV). Its extension to linear-quadratic optimal control is the succinct LQR value problem (SLQRV). We prove that SLV is $\BQP$-hard: every problem in bounded-error quantum polynomial time ($\BQP$) reduces to it in polynomial time. We then establish that the more general SLQRV problem admits a quantum algorithm running in time polynomial in the succinct input length. Since SLV is a special case of SLQRV, both problems are $\BQP$-complete. Consequently, unless bounded-error probabilistic polynomial time coincides with $\BQP$, no classical randomized algorithm can solve either problem on all promised instances in time polynomial in the succinct input length.
item.dc:creator: Mohamed Serry, Jun Liu

item.title: Pricing Short-Circuit Current via a Primal-Dual Formulation for Preserving Integrality Constraints
item.description: arXiv:2510.05293v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Synchronous Generators (SGs) currently provide important levels of Short-Circuit Current (SCC), a critical ancillary service that ensures line protections trip during short-circuit faults. Given the ongoing replacement of SGs by power-electronics-based generation, which has a hard limit on current injection, it has become relevant to optimize the procurement of SCC services provided by remaining SGs. Pricing this service, i.e., computing dual variables of SCC constraints, is however challenging due to the integrality constraints in Unit Commitment (UC). Existing methods, e.g., dispatchable pricing and restricted pricing, attempt to address this issue but exhibit limitations in handling non-convexities, resulting in SCC prices that either fail to cover the operating costs of units or lack interpretability. To overcome these pitfalls, we adopt a primal-dual formulation of the existing SCC-constrained dispatch that preserves the binary UC for effectively computing shadow prices of SCC services. Using a modified IEEE 30-bus system, the proposed method is compared with the previously developed pricing schemes. It is demonstrated that, under the proposed pricing method, revenue-adequate and explicit service prices can be assigned without the need for make-whole payments, an advantage that cannot be achieved by other pricing approaches.
item.dc:creator: Peng Wang, Luis Badesa

item.title: All-Pass Function OPF: A Solver-Friendly, Physics-Preserving Approximation of AC OPF
item.description: arXiv:2601.14468v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper presents a rational approximation of the AC optimal power flow (AC OPF) problem based on an all-pass approximation of the exponential power flow kernel. The classical AC OPF relies on trigonometric coupling between bus voltage phasors, which yields a nonconvex program with oscillatory derivatives that can slow, or in some cases destabilize, interior-point methods. We replace the trigonometric terms with an all-pass function (APF) approximation whose real and imaginary components act as smooth surrogates for the cosine and sine functions, and we introduce a pre-rotation to shift the argument of the approximation toward its most accurate region, ensuring that the reformulated power flow model preserves physical loss behavior, maintains the symmetry of the classical kernels, and improves the conditioning of the Jacobian and Hessian matrices. The proposed APF OPF formulation remains nonconvex, as in the classical model, but it eliminates trigonometric evaluations and empirically produces larger and more stable Newton steps under standard interior-point solvers. Numerical results on more than 25 IEEE and PGLib test systems ranging from 9 to 10{,}000 buses demonstrate that the APF OPF model achieves solutions with accuracy comparable to that of the classical formulation while reducing solver times, indicating a more solver-friendly nonconvex representation of AC OPF. All code, functions, verification scripts, and generated results are publicly available on \href{https://github.com/LSU-RAISE-LAB/APF-OPF}{GitHub}, along with a README describing how to run and reproduce the experiments.
item.dc:creator: Milad Hasanzadeh, Amin Kargarian, Javad Lavaei

item.title: Challenges in the Proper Metrological Verification of Smart Energy Meters
item.description: arXiv:2601.16612v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The most common instruments currently used to measure active/reactive energy and power quality indicators are smart energy meters (EM). Unfortunately, the verification of such meters is currently performed under ideal conditions or with simple signal models, which do not recreate actual states occurring in the power grid and do not ensure the verification of the properties of their signal chains. This paper presents challenges in proper metrological verification of smart EM. It presents existing legal and normative requirements and scientific research directions regarding these meters. Although the meters tested comply with the normative and legal requirements, the results reveal numerous imperfections in the signal and measurement chains for the selected test signal. Based on the results of the research results, further directions have been determined in the field of smart EM.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: A. Bracale, J. Janowicz, P. Kuwa{\l}ek and G. Wiczy\'nski, "Challenges in the Proper Metrological Verification of Smart Energy Meters," 2026 22nd ICHQP, Dresden, Germany, 2026
item.dc:creator: Antonio Bracale, Jakub Janowicz, Piotr Kuwa{\l}ek, Grzegorz Wiczy\'nski

item.title: Low-Thrust Trajectory Optimization for Cubesat Lunar Mission: HORYU-VI
item.description: arXiv:2602.16831v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A three-stage low-thrust trajectory is investigated for the HORYU-VI CubeSat lunar mission: pre-flyby deceleration, lunar capture, and orbit circularization. Impulsive reference trajectories initialize finite-burn targeting in the General Mission Analysis Tool (GMAT). The archived case uses constant 12 kg spacecraft mass and 1.08 mN effective thrust. The first reported bound lunar state occurs at day 184.1. At the end of the 381.3-day record, the osculating lunar orbit has semi-major axis 3,862 km and eccentricity 0.0867. Integrating the reported thrust state yields an estimated velocity increment of 839.8 m/s over 108.00 days of thrust. At the configured 2800 s specific impulse, the ideal rocket-equation propellant equivalent is 0.361 kg; mass depletion was disabled in the propagation. The record demonstrates lunar capture and partial circularization. Completion of the intended 100 km science orbit, coupled mass-depleting propagation, and uncertainty analysis remain necessary to assess operational feasibility.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Proceedings of the 71st International Astronautical Congress (IAC), The CyberSpace Edition, 12-14 October 2020, paper IAC-20-C1,4,8,x55549
item.dc:creator: Omer Burak Iskender, Keck Voon Ling, Mengu Cho, Sangkyun Kim, Necmi Cihan Orger

item.title: Over-the-Air Consensus-based Formation Control of Heterogeneous Agents: Communication-Rate and Geometry-Aware Convergence Guarantees
item.description: arXiv:2603.10245v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper investigates the formation control problem of heterogeneous, autonomous agents that communicate over a wireless multiple access channel. Instead of avoiding interference through orthogonal node-to-node transmissions, we exploit the superposition property of the wireless channel to compute, at each receiver, normalized convex combinations of simultaneously broadcast neighbor signals. At every communication instant, agents update their reference positions from these aggregates, and track the references in continuous time between updates. The only assumption on the agent dynamics is that each agent tracks constant reference positions exponentially, which accommodates a broad class of platforms. Under this assumption, we analyze the resulting jump-flow system under time-varying communication graphs and unknown channel coefficients. We derive a communication-rate based sufficient condition that guarantees convergence to a prescribed formation. We then provide a geometry-aware refinement showing how favorable tracking transients can relax the required condition. Simulations with unicycle agents illustrate the theoretical results and demonstrate a substantial reduction in the number of required orthogonal transmissions compared to interference-avoiding node-to-node communication protocols.
item.dc:creator: Michael Epp, Fabio Molinari, J\"org Raisch

item.title: Scaling and Trade-offs in Multi-agent Autonomous Systems
item.description: arXiv:2603.10743v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Designing autonomous drone swarms is hampered by a vast design space spanning platform, algorithmic, and numerical-strength choices. We perform large-scale agent-based simulations in three canonical scenarios: swarm-on-swarm battle, cooperative area search with attrition, and pursuit of scattering targets. We demonstrate how dimensional-analysis and data-scaling can be leveraged to collapse performance data onto scaling functions that are mathematically simple, yet counterintuitive and therefore difficult to predict a priori. These scaling laws reveal success-failure boundaries, including sharp break points which we show can be framed as an ``effective swarm size.'' Additionally, we show how this technique can be used to quantify trade-offs between agent count and platform parameters such as velocity, sensing or weapon range, and attrition rate. Furthermore, we show the benefits of embedding an optimal path planning loop within this framework, which can qualitatively improve the scaling laws that govern the outcome. The methods we demonstrate are highly flexible and would enable rapid, budget-aware sizing and algorithm selection for large autonomous swarms.
item.dc:creator: Abram H. Clark, Liraz Mudrik, Colton Kawamura, Nathan C. Redder, Jo\~ao P. Hespanha, Isaac Kaminer

item.title: Conformalized Data-Driven Reachability Analysis with PAC Guarantees
item.description: arXiv:2603.12220v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Data-driven reachability analysis computes reachable sets directly from noisy data. Existing matrix-zonotope reachability methods require a known noise bound, and their nonlinear extensions require a Lipschitz constant. We propose Conformalized Data-Driven Reachability, which calibrates the open-loop prediction error of a least-squares model with training-conditional split conformal prediction and propagates the initial set and the input set with zonotopes. The resulting sets contain the whole trajectory with a probably approximately correct (PAC) guarantee that requires only independent and identically distributed trajectories, and the number of calibration trajectories does not depend on the horizon. The prediction error depends on the initial states and the controller only through the model error. The method extends to measurement noise with a known quantile and to nonlinear systems through local affine models. In experiments, the sets keep an average coverage above 99% when the initial states and the controller change, whereas sets calibrated directly on the states lose coverage.
item.dc:creator: Yanliang Huang, Zhen Zhang, Peng Xie, Zhuoqi Zeng, Amr Alanwar

item.title: Certified Set Convergence for Piecewise Affine Systems
item.description: arXiv:2604.00286v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: When all individuals of a system receive the same input, one open-loop input sequence has to steer every possible initial state to a target. We study this problem for piecewise affine systems with bounded disturbances, where every state of an initial box must reach a robustly invariant target. When the reachable set crosses a switching surface, it splits into fragments that follow different dynamics, and existing set-based controllers then give each fragment its own state feedback, which a common input does not allow. Instead, we propose a planner-independent and sound verification framework for common-input control of disturbed piecewise affine systems. Any planner can propose candidate sequences, and the verifier certifies a sequence by following every fragment under the dynamics of its own region. To certify all possible initial boxes in a given range, we partition the range into finitely many cells and certify each cell. On three evaluation systems, every possible initial box in the considered ranges is certified.
item.dc:creator: Yanliang Huang, Peng Xie, Zhen Zhang, Wenyuan Wu, Zhuoqi Zeng, Amr Alanwar

item.title: Scalable Optimization for Mobility-Aware Coordinated Electric Vehicle Charging in Power Distribution Networks
item.description: arXiv:2604.11999v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Rapid growth in electric-vehicle (EV) charging demand is placing increasing stress on power distribution networks (PDNs), whose hosting capacity is often limited and spatially uneven. Beyond demonstrating that coordination can help, this paper answers an open question that is central for planners: What is the maximal achievable benefit of EV charging demand flexibility from spatial and temporal shifting in reducing overload-driven distribution upgrades at a regional scale? We introduce MAC (Mobility-Aware Coordinated EV charging) to establish a credible upper bound, which entails rethinking charging flexibility around individual mobility, fusing travel itineraries with feeder-level hosting-capacity data, and solving population-scale optimization with spatio-temporal coupling to certified near-optimality. (i) MAC expands feasible scheduling by coupling charging decisions over the full mobility horizon. Instead of enforcing per-session energy recovery, it only requires the EV state-of-charge (SOC) to remain sufficient for upcoming trips. (ii) MAC is computationally scalable via an iterated price response (IPR) scheme. Each iteration posts a locational-temporal price, collects the fleet's best responses in parallel, and updates the price from the observed capacity shortage. Custom batched subproblem solvers remove the per-iteration bottleneck of solving millions of best responses. In a future-oriented 30% EV adoption scenario for the San Francisco Bay Area, MAC almost eliminates overload-driven upgrade needs relative to unmanaged charging. Comparing across the baseline spectrum, mobility-aware flexibility alone removes most of the overload, outperforming even fully coordinated session-based charging, and coordination on top suppresses most of the remainder. Both levers are thus essential, and the resulting best-case benchmarks provide references for PDN planning and operations.
item.dc:creator: Yi Ju, Lunlong Li, Jingchun Wang, Scott Moura

item.title: Lipschitz-Guided Machine Learning Framework for Accelerating Transient Stability Analysis of Flexible Traction Power Supply Systems
item.description: arXiv:2606.00883v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The rapidly varying and moving train loads in electrified railways impose stringent requirements on the transient stability of flexible traction power supply systems (FTPSSs). However, the complex dynamic interactions among numerous traction substations (TSs) make it challenging for existing transient stability analysis (TSA) methods to achieve both high accuracy and computational efficiency. To bridge this gap, this paper proposes a Lipschitz-guided machine learning framework that leverages Lipschitz continuity to restructure the transient stability verification of FTPSSs. By replacing computationally intensive satisfiability modulo theories (SMT) solvers with a deterministic algebraic check on a finite mesh, the proposed method ensures the Lyapunov conditions between mesh points without simplifications of the FTPSS dynamics. Validated on FTPSSs with three to five TSs through extensive case studies, the proposed framework accelerates training by up to 12 times compared with SMT-based neural Lyapunov methods and certifies the five-TS system. Furthermore, the proposed framework achieves up to a 33.5-fold increase in the estimated region of attraction (ROA) compared with linear matrix inequality.This advancement provides an efficient TSA solution for droop-controlled FTPSSs.
item.dc:creator: Zhong Liu, Jialin Zheng, Xiaonan Lu

item.title: Measure the Deployment, Not Just the Model: Rethinking Hardware-Aware Model Selection for Microcontrollers
item.description: arXiv:2606.15004v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Selecting an energy-efficient model for periodic sensing requires accounting for time between inferences. Hardware-aware model search typically measures inference alone, even when the application cares about energy per release. We present CREST (Cross-platform Runtime Evaluation and Search Tool), an open-source hardware-in-the-loop experimentation system that evaluates model and hardware configurations under a specified release schedule. Researchers can vary the objective, schedule, target and candidate proposer while reusing evaluation and replay. Records preserve comparison conditions and separate valid measurements from deployable candidates. Three case studies demonstrate the system. First, searches and controlled replay on STM32 N657 show how waiting changes model and clock selection. For one architecture, continuous inference favors 800 MHz over 300 MHz at 8.0 versus 17.1 mJ per inference, but additional waiting offsets 97% of this saving in a fitted decomposition. With STOP between releases, 300 MHz uses about 0.3-0.4% less board energy per release at 100 and 500 ms. At a fixed clock, the preferred architecture changes between release periods, which a model with shared waiting parameters cannot produce. Latency predicts continuous energy within a median 1.7% on held-out observations, yet most release-energy error remains in scheduled terms. In paired replay, one of six randomly selected near-latency pairs reverses its continuous-energy order by 5.8 mJ per release. Second, replay on three Arduino targets shows proxy-selected inertial-odometry candidates can fail to fit or use more energy than measured selections, with only 9 of 16 FLOPs-selected candidates fitting the most memory-constrained board. Third, an audio classification study reuses the evaluator with LLM-based candidate proposers, and cross-target replay moves a selected configuration from third to last in energy rank.
item.dc:creator: Joseph Q. Zales, Pragya Sharma, Mani Srivastava

item.title: Robust Adaptive Backup Control Barrier Functions
item.description: arXiv:2607.20842v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We propose a notion of robust adaptive backup control barrier functions for nonlinear control affine systems with parametric uncertainty in both the drift dynamics and actuation matrix. Backup control barrier functions guarantee safety by predicting the system's trajectory under a pre-certified safe controller. However, these predictions rely on the model and can be inaccurate when the system contains unknown parameters. To address this issue, we estimate the unknown parameters using element-wise certified adaptive estimators that provide a parameter adaptation law and component-wise estimation error bounds. We compute the backup flow using the estimated model and tighten the safety conditions using these certified bounds. The resulting safety conditions account for the sensitivity of the predicted flow to parameter estimation errors. Moreover, to handle uncertainty in the actuation matrix, we use a duality-based reformulation that enables the use of a computationally efficient quadratic-program-based safety filter. We prove that controllers satisfying the proposed robust adaptive backup control barrier function constraints guarantee safety under parametric uncertainty and input constraints.
item.dc:creator: Ersin Da\c{s}, David E. J. van Wijk, Tamas G. Molnar, Aaron D. Ames, Joel W. Burdick

item.title: Digital Twin Networks for 6G Wireless Systems: Architecture, Enabling Technologies, AI-Driven Control, and Open Challenges
item.description: arXiv:2608.12267v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The transition to the Sixth Generation (6G) of mobile networks requires proactive and deterministic orchestration to satisfy the stringent key performance indicators of future services, including ultra-reliable low-latency communications, enhanced mobile broadband, and massive machine-type communications. Digital Twin Networks (DTNs) have emerged as a foundational technology to meet these demands, offering real-time and high-fidelity virtual replicas of the physical network. Although the literature explores DTNs conceptually, a gap exists in the coverage of technical classification and computational feasibility evaluations. This survey addresses this gap by formally categorizing state-of-the-art DTN architectures into passive monitoring twins and active control twins. We evaluate their enabling technologies, namely ray-tracing, reconfigurable intelligent surfaces, artificial intelligence, and multi-access edge computing. Importantly, we analyze the complexity of ten state-of-the-art frameworks, five reporting complexity expressions, four derived in this survey, and one not derivable, to assess hardware scalability and inference bottlenecks. These architectures are then linked to forthcoming 6G use cases, including smart cities, Industry 5.0, healthcare, and smart grids. Finally, we synthesize crucial unresolved challenges, highlighting graphics processing unit hardware limitations, cyber-physical actuation latency, and the need for a zero-trust security paradigm, offering research directions toward the unified Internet of Everything.
item.dc:creator: Charalampos Oikonomidis, Emmanouel T. Michailidis, Demosthenes Vouyioukas, Nikolaos I. Miridakis

item.title: Industrial Load Modeling and Optimization for Market-Based Interaction with Power Systems
item.description: arXiv:2608.15076v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The transition toward a renewable-dominated power system increases the flexibility needed to balance net-load variations. Industrial loads account for over 40% of the world's electricity consumption and can shift large amounts of demand through automated production scheduling. However, making industrial processes a dependable flexibility resource for power systems remains challenging, because industrial process constraints are non-convex, equipment parameters are often private, and device-level models of thousands of facilities are too detailed for aggregator and power-system optimization. This dissertation builds computationally efficient methods for modeling and optimizing industrial flexibility for power-system interaction. Specifically, this dissertation uses smart meters as the external measurement interface and maps industrial process constraints into a concise flexibility space for electricity-market operation. The resulting chain of mechanism modeling, parameter identification, constraint dimension reduction, and optimal decision-making makes industrial-load participation computationally tractable while retaining precise process models for final execution.
item.dc:creator: Ruike Lyu

item.title: From Winding-Fault Geometry to Reliability: Estimation and Prognosis of Stator Inter-Turn Faults
item.description: arXiv:2609.13448v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper develops an integrated framework for estimation, prognosis, and reliability assessment of stator inter-turn faults in induction motors. The fault is characterized by its severity, defined as the fraction of short-circuited turns, and its spatial orientation. A geometric fault model shows that the resulting output signature is affine in the fault severity and exhibits a fundamental spatial periodicity. Exploiting this structure, an augmented-state particle filter jointly estimates the nonlinear electromechanical state and the unknown fault severity while quantifying posterior uncertainty. The estimated degradation is then propagated using four prognostic models: linear trend, Holt exponential smoothing, Bayesian degradation, and particle-based forecasting. Their predictions are connected to threshold-crossing remaining useful life (RUL), first-passage reliability, degradation-dependent hazard reliability, and a Weibull lifetime benchmark, thereby providing both deterministic and probabilistic health assessments. Numerical results demonstrate accurate online fault estimation and output reconstruction, characterize the effects of degradation pattern and prediction horizon on prognosis, and show consistent reliability and threshold-crossing predictions. Moreover, estimation accuracy remains comparable across the distinct fault orientations induced by the spatial periodicity. The resulting framework provides a unified connection from physics-based inter-turn fault modeling to online diagnosis, degradation prognosis, and reliability assessment.
item.dc:creator: Bambang L. Widjiantoro, Syahrul Munir, Katherin Indriawati, Moh Kamalul Wafi

item.title: On asymptotic stability of the time-varying Kalman filter for unstabilizable linear systems: an optimization perspective
item.description: arXiv:2609.18925v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper establishes the necessary and sufficient conditions for asymptotic stability of the time-varying Kalman filter applied to a linear time invariant system with semidefinite initial state covariance and positive definite process and measurement noise. Rather than analyze the discrete Riccati equation as in the classic literature, the equivalent state smoothing optimization problem is stated and all results are established using properties of this optimization problem. A Lyapunov-like function, termed a modified $Q$-function is derived and used for this analysis. This optimization approach removes the need for the classic but cumbersome Riccati iteration algebra and provides better generalization and application for nonlinear systems.
item.dc:creator: James B. Rawlings, Titus Quah, Matthias A. M\"uller

item.title: Interconnections of Dissipative Networks Through a Dynamic Scattering Controller
item.description: arXiv:2609.21934v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The problem of modular scattering-based design of dissipative networks is addressed. Under basic assumptions imposed on subsystems, design of a dynamic scattering-based interconnection controller is proposed which guarantees that the resulting interconnection is internally stable and possesses the same set of basic properties as the individual subsystems. This enables iterative application of the developed technique, which allows for building of large-scale dissipative networks in a modular fashion. The proposed method provides substantial flexibility in the controller design as well as in the choice of input and output signals used for interconnections.
item.dc:creator: Ilia G. Polushin

item.title: Price-Optimized EV and Heat-Pump Scheduling Can Exceed Uncoordinated Feeder Peaks
item.description: arXiv:2610.05916v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Electric vehicles and heat pumps add large, time-flexible loads to low-voltage feeders. When each household independently minimizes its own charging cost against the same electricity price, this flexible demand piles into the cheapest hours, and the resulting synchronization can stress the feeder more than uncoordinated operation does. This work quantifies that effect on a rural low-voltage feeder with photovoltaics (97 buses, 250 kVA transformer) in 913 simulation runs that compare seven strategies across four seasons, device penetrations of up to 90 %, 208 price weeks from 2022-2025, and heterogeneous heat pumps. At 30 % penetration of each device, this decentralized cost minimization drives the transformer to 253 % of rated capacity, more than three times the peak of non-optimized Fixed-random charging with the same mobility and charged energy, and 478 % with electric vehicles alone at 90 % penetration, with undervoltage at the far end of the longest feeder arm. It exceeds Fixed-random and Fixed-times charging in every winter, spring, and autumn price week, and each 30 pp of heat-pump penetration raises its peak by about 110 pp, twelve times as much as without optimization. Centralized peak minimization removes all demand-driven violations. In the heat-pump-free summer case at 60 % photovoltaics, midday reverse power flow sets a transformer floor of 128.9 % that no strategy undercuts, since no commuting electric vehicle is at home at the export peak. With a time-variable grid fee added to the spot price, the weekly peak of decentralized cost minimization falls into the reduced-fee window in 99 of the 104 fee-active price weeks, compared with 53 without the fee, while keeping at least 89.8 % of its height, so the fee relocates rather than removes the synchronization. The simulation and optimization code is available at https://github.com/lukas-wagner/SynchronizationEffectsAnalysis.
item.dc:creator: Tatjana Hein, Lukas P. Wagner, Alex Bernhard, Felix Ocker

item.title: First-order plants are globally asymptotically stable under antithetic feedback
item.description: arXiv:2610.06608v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We show that first-order linear plants are globally asymptotically stable under antithetic feedback. This is shown by constructing an explicit smooth, convex Lyapunov function and by appealing to a Krasovskii-LaSalle invariance principle.
item.dc:creator: Wouter Jongeneel

item.title: Equilibria and Consensus in Mixed Weighted-Average and Weighted-Median Opinion Dynamics: The Consensus-Promoting Role of Weighted-Average Individuals
item.description: arXiv:2610.16406v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: How individuals respond to their neighbors' opinions shapes whether a networked group reaches consensus. This paper analyzes synchronous discrete-time opinion dynamics on a fixed influence network, where individuals use either weighted-average (WA) or weighted-median (WM) opinion-aggregation mechanisms with individual-specific inertia coefficients. We characterize equilibria through graph-theoretic conditions on opinion level sets and WA balance equations, proving that every solution converges to a Lyapunov-stable equilibrium. We define type-dependent cohesive sets, whose WA members assign all their influence weight to the set and WM members assign at least half. The absence of two disjoint such sets gives a necessary and sufficient graph-theoretic criterion for consensus from any initial condition. Otherwise, an open set of initial conditions leads to persistent dissensus. Converting WM individuals to WA cannot create type-dependent cohesive sets and preserves existing guarantees of consensus from any initial condition. If the conversion eliminates every disjoint pair of these sets, the converted system also guarantees consensus from any initial condition. Four numerical studies examine the locations and proportion of weighted-average individuals, as well as the influence weights, while comparing the consensus criterion with finite-horizon simulation outcomes. In the four network ensembles with 100 individuals, the observed frequency of reaching a prescribed consensus tolerance is nondecreasing with WA proportion at each tested simulation horizon. This trend supports the consensus-promoting role of WA individuals, although individual realizations need not follow it.
item.dc:creator: Junkai Cheng, Wenjun Mei

item.title: Anytime-Valid Runtime Monitoring of Learned Barrier Certificates
item.description: arXiv:2610.27726v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Learned barrier certificates provide a principled mechanism for establishing safety of stochastic systems, but their validity may deteriorate during deployment when the underlying dynamics differ from those used for training. We propose an anytime-valid runtime monitor that audits a learned barrier certificate using observed closed-loop trajectories. The monitor is intended to detect loss of statistical support for the deployed barrier condition; it does not by itself guarantee detection before unsafe entry or safety of a subsequent intervention. Specifically, the conditional barrier-drift condition is formulated as an episode-wise sequential hypothesis test, and observed barrier increments are transformed into a nonnegative test supermartingale, yielding finite-sample false-alarm control under arbitrary stopping times. Inspired by finite-horizon safety verification, we further introduce a deterministic temporal shaping of the monitoring boundary, making the monitor more conservative early in a prescribed deployment horizon while preserving anytime-validity. The monitor is designed to detect statistical evidence that the safety certificate is no longer consistent with the observed dynamics, rather than to predict unsafe entry. To assess the monitor empirically, we evaluate empirical alarm behavior under valid and invalid certificates. Code and data are available at https://github.com/FormalCert-AI/runtime-barrier-monitor.
item.dc:creator: Zhipeng Cao, Taoran Wu, Weiru Cui, Luke Ong, Bai Xue

item.title: Learning-Oriented Fault-Tolerant Control for UAVs with Time-Varying Fault Estimation
item.description: arXiv:2610.30566v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The increasing deployment of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) in safety-critical applications has created a growing demand for control strategies that remain reliable in the presence of actuator and sensor faults. This paper presents a fault-tolerant control framework that combines constructive mathematical modeling, proportional--integral (PI) fault estimation, and learning-oriented control. A nonlinear quadcopter model is first developed using both the Newton--Euler and Euler--Lagrange formulations, from which a discrete-time linear model is derived for observer and controller design.
